Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 39, verse 5:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He created the heavens and the earth with truth﴾ [meaning]: He did not create them for nothing.

(p-163) ﴿He wraps the night over the day﴾. Abu 'Ubayda said: He makes this enter upon that. Ibn Qutayba said: The origin of takwir (wrapping) is winding, and from it comes "kawwara al-'imama" (he wound the turban). Others said: Takwir is placing one thing over another.

﴿And He subjected the sun and the moon﴾, meaning: He made them submissive to moving according to His will. ﴿Each runs for a specified term﴾, meaning: until the term that Allah set for the world. We have already explained the meaning of al-'Aziz in [al-Baqara: 129] and the meaning of al-Ghaffar in [Ta-Ha: 82].

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 39, verse 6:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He created you from a single soul﴾, meaning Adam, ﴿then made from it its mate﴾. That is: before your creation He made from it its mate, because Hawwa' (Eve) was created before the offspring. A similar usage in speech is for you to say: "I have given you something today, and then what I gave you yesterday is more." This is the view chosen by al-Farra' (the grammarian). Others said: "Then He informed you that He created from it its mate." ﴿And He sent down for you of the cattle﴾, that is, He created ﴿eight pairs﴾, and we have explained them in surah al-An'am [6:143].

﴿Creation after creation﴾, that is: drops of sperm, then a clot, then a lump of flesh chewed-like, then bone, then flesh, then hair grew, and beyond that the various changes of state until the bringing forth of children. This is the view of the majority (al-Jumhur). Ibn Zayd said: "Creation in the bellies after your creation in the loins of Adam."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿in three darknesses﴾: the darkness of the belly, the darkness of the womb, and the darkness of the placenta (p-164). This was said by the majority, and Ibn Zayd agreed with them. Abu 'Ubayda said: they are the darkness of the father's loins, the darkness of the mother's belly, and the darkness of the womb.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then how are you turned away?﴾, that is: from where are you turned away from the path of truth after this clarification?!

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 39, verse 7:

﴿If you disbelieve, then indeed Allah is free of need of you﴾, meaning: free of need of your faith and your worship. ﴿And He does not approve for His servants disbelief﴾. There are two views concerning this. The first is that He does not approve it for the believers, as said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second is that He does not approve it for anyone, even if it occurs by His will (irada). There is a difference between will (irada) and approval (ridha). We have pointed to this in [al-Baqarah: 205] at His words: ﴿And Allah does not love corruption﴾.

﴿And if you are grateful, He approves it for you﴾, meaning He approves that gratitude for you. ﴿Indeed, He is Knowing of what is in the breasts﴾, meaning of what is in the hearts.

(p-165) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when harm touches man﴾. The scholars differ over who this verse was revealed about, and there are two views. The first is that it was about Utba ibn Rabi'a, related by 'Ata'. The second is that it was about Abu Hudhayfa ibn al-Mughira, related by Muqatil. *Ad-durr* (harm) means trial and hardship.

﴿Turning penitently to Him﴾, that is, returning to Him from his polytheism.

﴿Then when He bestows upon him﴾, that is, gives him and grants him, ﴿a favour from Himself﴾ after the trial that befell him, such as health after sickness or wealth after poverty, ﴿he forgets﴾, that is, he abandons what he used to call upon. There are three views on this. The first is that he forgot the supplication with which he used to humble himself before Allah, Exalted is He. The second is that he forgot the harm from which he used to ask Allah to relieve him. The third is that he forgot Allah, to whom he used to humble himself. Al-Zajjaj said: *ma* may refer to Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, as in His saying: ﴿nor will you worship what I worship﴾ (al-Kafirun: 3). Al-Farra' said: he abandoned what he used to call upon. The meaning of *al-andad* (equals or rivals to Allah) has already been explained (al-Baqarah: 22), as has the meaning of ﴿so that he may lead (others) astray from the way of Allah﴾ (al-Hajj: 9).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "Enjoy your disbelief for a while."﴾ Its wording is that of a command, but its meaning is a threat. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿Enjoy, then you will come to know﴾ (al-Nahl: 55).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 39, verse 9–10:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient (qanit) during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing...﴾ Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Hamzah, Abu Ja'far, al-Mufaddal from Asim, and Zayd from Ya'qub read "Amin" with a light (takhfif) pronunciation. The rest read it with a doubled (tashdid) pronunciation. As for the doubled reading, its meaning is: "Is this which we have mentioned better, or one who is devoutly obedient?" The original form of "amman" is "am man," and the mim was assimilated into the mim.

As for the light reading, there are three possible interpretations of it.

The first: it carries the sense of a call (nida'). Al-Farra' said: "Those who read it this way explained it as: O one who is devoutly obedient..., and this is a good interpretation. The Arabs address someone with the alif just as they address with the particle ya, saying: 'Ya Zayd, aqbil' and 'Azayd, aqbil'." So the meaning is that He mentioned the forgetful disbeliever, then related the account of the righteous person by way of address, as you would say: "So-and-so does not fast and does not pray, so O one who fasts, rejoice!"

The second: its implied sense is: "Is one who is devoutly obedient like one who is not devoutly obedient?!"

The third: "Is one who is devoutly obedient like one who has set up rivals to Allah?!"

We have already mentioned the meaning of qunut (devout obedience) in [al-Baqarah: 116] and the meaning of ﴿during the hours of the night﴾ in [Al 'Imran: 113].

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿prostrating and standing﴾ means in prayer. There are five opinions regarding who this verse was revealed about. The first: it is Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, narrated by Ata' from Ibn Abbas. The second: Uthman ibn Affan, said by Ibn Umar. The third: Ammar ibn Yasir, said by Muqatil. The fourth: Ibn Mas'ud, Ammar, Suhayb, and Abu Dharr, said by Ibn al-Sa'ib. The fifth: that it is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), related by Yahya ibn Salam.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿fearing the Hereafter﴾ means the punishment of the Hereafter. Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Ibn Abbas, Urwah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu Raja', and Abu Imran read: "yuhadhdhiru 'adhab al-akhirah" with the addition of "adhab."

﴿and hoping for the mercy of his Lord﴾ On this there are two opinions. The first: it is forgiveness, said by Ibn al-Sa'ib. The second: it is Paradise, said by Muqatil.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: Are those who know equal to those who do not know?﴾ That what Allah promised of reward (thawab) and punishment ('iqab) is true. ﴿and those who do not know⦆ The rest of the verse has already been discussed in [al-Ra'd: 19], and likewise His saying: ﴿For those who do good in this world there is good﴾ has been discussed in [al-Nahl: 30].

Regarding His saying: ﴿And Allah's earth is spacious﴾ there are two opinions. The first: it urges them to emigrate from Mecca to wherever they may be safe. The second: it is the land of Paradise, encouraging them toward it.

﴿Only the patient will be paid their reward in full⦆ those who were patient for the sake of Allah, Exalted is He, over what afflicted them, ﴿without reckoning⦆ meaning: they will be given a great reward, too vast to be counted and too great to be encompassed, not in proportion to their deeds.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 39, verse 19–20:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Is then one against whom the word of punishment has become due...﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: It had already been decreed in Allah's knowledge that he would be in the Fire.

If it is said: how do two interrogatives without an answer come together in this verse?

It is said: As for al-Farraʾ, he says: This is one of the cases where only one interrogative is intended, but the interrogative particle has been moved out of its proper place, so it is returned to its place. The meaning becomes: "Can you rescue those who are in the Fire, those against whom the word of punishment has become due?" A similar example is ﴿Does he promise you that when you die and become dust and bones, you will be brought forth?﴾ [al-Muʾminun: 35], where he repeated "annakum" twice, and the meaning is: "Does he promise you that you will be brought forth when you have died?" Another similar example is ﴿Do not think that those who rejoice in what they have brought...﴾, then He said: ﴿So do not think them...﴾ [Al ʿImran: 188], where he repeated "tahsabanna" twice, and the meaning is: "Do not think that those who rejoice in what they have brought are secure from punishment." Al-Zajjaj said: It is possible that there is an omitted element in the speech, its estimate being: "Is then one against whom the word of punishment has become due, so that he is freed from it or saved, [can you save him]? Can you rescue him?" The exegetes said: "Can you free him from what has been decreed for him, so that you make him a believer?" The meaning is: you have no power to do that. ʿAta said: By this verse he means Abu Lahab, his son, and those of the Prophet's ﷺ kin who stayed away from faith.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But those who feared their Lord﴾. Abu al-Mutawakkil and Abu Jaʿfar read "lakinna" with the nun doubled [and with a fatha]. Al-Zajjaj said: "al-Ghuraf" are the lofty dwellings in Paradise. ﴿Above them are lofty chambers﴾, meaning: dwellings higher than them.

﴿Promise of Allah﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar); the meaning is: Allah promised them chambers as a promise. And whoever reads "waʿdu Allah" with the damma, the meaning is: that is the promise of Allah.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 39, verse 21:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He sends down water from the sky﴾. Al-Sha'bi said: Everything on the earth comes down from the sky. ﴿Then He makes it flow as springs﴾. Ibn Qutayba said: That is, He makes it enter and turns it into springs, meaning gushing fountains. ﴿Then it dries up﴾, that is, it becomes dry. Al-Asma'i said: It is said of a plant when its dryness is complete: "qad hāja yahīju hayjan" (it has dried up, becoming withered).

As for al-ḥuṭām (debris, dry crumbled stalks), Abu 'Ubayda said: It is what has dried up and broken off into pieces from the plants, and its like is al-rufāt (crumbled remains). Muqatil said: This is a parable that God struck for the worldly life: while you see the plant green, it changes, dries up, and then perishes, and likewise is the world and its adornment. Others said: This explanation serves to show the power of God, Mighty and Majestic.

(p-173) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Is one whose breast Allah has opened to Islam...﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: Its answer is omitted, because the context indicates it. Its estimated meaning is: "Is one whose breast Allah has opened, so that he is guided, like one upon whose heart a seal has been set, so that he is not guided?" This is indicated by His saying: ﴿So woe to those whose hearts are hardened﴾. Ibn Mas'ud related that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse, and we said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what is this opening (sharh)?'" and he mentioned a hadith that we have already mentioned in His saying: ﴿So whoever Allah wants to guide, He opens his breast to Islam﴾ [al-An'am: 125].

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He is upon a light﴾. On this there are four opinions. The first: certainty (yaqin), said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: the Book of Allah, which he holds to and to which he turns, said by Qatadah. The third: clear explanation (bayan), said by Ibn al-Sa'ib. The fourth: guidance (huda), said by Muqatil.

(p-174) Concerning whom was this verse revealed? On this there are three opinions.

The first: that it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and Ubayy ibn Khalaf. Al-Dahhak related it from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: concerning 'Ali, Hamzah, Abu Lahab and his son, said by 'Ata'.

The third: concerning the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and Abu Jahl, said by Muqatil.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So woe to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah﴾. We have already explained the meaning of hardness (qasawah) in [al-Baqarah: 74].

If it is said: How can the heart become hard from the remembrance of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic?

The answer: Whenever the remembrance of Allah, which they deny, is recited to them, their hearts become hardened against faith in it. Muqatil and others held that "min" (from) here means "'an" (from/against). Al-Farra' said: just as you say "atkhamtu 'an ta'amin akaltahu" (I became overfull because of a food I ate) and "atkhamtu min ta'amin akaltahu" (I became overfull from a food I ate). Their hearts became hard "min the remembrance of Allah" because they made it a lie, so it hardened their hearts. Whoever says "their hearts became hard against it" means: they turned away from it. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Ibn Abi 'Ablah and Abu 'Imran read: "قُلُوبُهم عَنِ ذِكْرِ اللَّهِ" (their hearts against the remembrance of Allah) in place of his saying "min".

(p-175) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah has sent down the best statement﴾ — meaning the Qur'an. We have already mentioned the occasion of its revelation at the beginning of [Surat] Yusuf.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿a Book, consistent, [in which] repetitions are made﴾. There are two views concerning it.

One: that some of it resembles other parts in its verses and letters; a verse resembles a verse, a word resembles a word, and a letter resembles a letter.

The second: that some of it confirms other parts, so there is in it no discrepancy and no contradiction.

It was said of it: ﴿repetitions﴾ because stories, obligatory duties, legal limits, reward and punishment are repeated in it.

If it is asked: what is the wisdom in repeating the stories, when a single telling would have sufficed?

The answer: the delegations of the Arabs would come to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the Muslims would recite to them some of the Qur'an, and that would suffice them. He used to send to the scattered tribes [copies of] different suras. Had the reports and stories not been repeated and reiterated, the story of Musa would have reached one people, the story of Isa another people, and the story of Nuh another people. So Allah, may He be exalted, willed to make these stories known across the corners of the earth and to bring them to every ear. As for the benefit of repeating the same kind of statement, such as His saying: "So which of the favours of your Lord will you deny?" [al-Rahman], and His saying: ﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾ [al-Kafirun], and His saying: ﴿Woe to you, and woe [again]﴾ [al-Qiyamah 34-35], and ﴿And what will make you know what the Day of Recompense is?﴾ [al-Infitar 17-18] — we will mention it in the commentary on Surat al-Rahman, the Mighty and Majestic.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The skins of those who fear their Lord shiver from it﴾ — meaning they are seized (p-176) by a shuddering, which is a change that occurs in the human skin from fear. Al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib narrated from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that he said: "When the skin of the servant shivers out of fear of Allah, his sins fall away as leaves fall from a dry tree."

There are three views on the meaning of the verse. One: they shiver at His threat and soften at His promise; this was said by al-Suddi. The second: they shiver from fear and soften from hope. The third: the skins shiver in awe of Him and soften when He is recited; Al-Mawardi mentioned these two.

Some scholars of meanings said: the object of "remembrance" in His saying ﴿to the remembrance of Allah﴾ is omitted, because it is known; and the meaning is: their hearts become tranquil at the remembrance of Allah — that is, Paradise and reward. Qatadah said: this is the description of the friends of Allah; their skins shiver [and their hearts soften], and He did not describe them as losing their minds or swooning. That is only among the people of innovation, and it is from Satan. Abu Hazim reported: Ibn Umar passed by a man from the people of Iraq who had collapsed, and he said: "What is his condition?" They said: "When the Qur'an is recited to him, this befalls him." He said: "Indeed we fear Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and we do not fall down." Amir ibn Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr said: I came to Ubayy, and he said to me: "Where were you?" I said: "I found a people, and I have never seen better than them, mentioning Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, so that one of them trembles until he swoons from fear of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. So I sat with them." He said: "Do not sit with them again, ever." He saw me (p-177) as though it had not affected me, and said: "I saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ reciting the Qur'an, and I saw Abu Bakr and Umar reciting the Qur'an, and this does not befall them from fear of Allah, the Exalted. Do you think they were more fearful of Allah than Abu Bakr and Umar?" He said: "So I saw it was as he said." Ikrimah said: Asma bint Abi Bakr was asked: did any of the early generation swoon from fear? She said: No, but they wept. Abdullah ibn Urwah ibn al-Zubayr said: I said to my grandmother Asma bint Abi Bakr: how did the companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ behave when the Qur'an was recited to them? She said: They were as Allah, the Exalted, described them: their eyes shed tears and their skins shivered. I said to her: today, when the Qur'an is recited to some people, one of them falls down swooning. She said: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. And there was a man who would tremble at the mention [of Allah]; Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said to him: "If you can control it, I do not mind that I do not count you [among us]; and if you cannot control it, then you have opposed those who came before you."

(p-178) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That is the guidance of Allah﴾ — concerning what is pointed to, there are two views. One: that it is the Qur'an; this was said by Muqatil. The second: that it is what befalls the believers when the Qur'an is recited, of the shivering of the skins at the threat and their softening at the promise; this was said by Ibn al-Anbari.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 39, verse 24–28:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is one who shields with his face from the terrible punishment﴾ — i.e., its severity. Al-Zajjaj said: its response is omitted, and its estimated meaning is: "Is he like one who enters Paradise?" It has come in the tafsir that the disbeliever is thrown into the Fire shackled, and he cannot shield himself from it except with his face.

Then He informed of what the guardians (al-khazana) say to the disbelievers, in His saying: ﴿And it will be said to the wrongdoers﴾ — meaning the disbelievers — ﴿Taste what you used to earn﴾ — i.e., the recompense of your earning.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those before them denied, so the punishment came to them from where they did not perceive﴾ — i.e., before them, the disbelievers of Makkah. ﴿So Allah made them taste disgrace﴾ — meaning humiliation and punishment, ﴿and the punishment of the Hereafter is greater﴾ than what befell them in the worldly life ﴿if they only knew﴾, but they do not know that.

﴿And We have certainly presented for the people in this Qur'an﴾ — i.e., We have described for them ﴿every kind of example﴾ — i.e., every kind of likeness resembling their circumstances.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿an Arabic Qur'an﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "Arabic" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). The meaning: We have presented for the people in this Qur'an while it is in its Arabic eloquence and clarity. So he mentioned "Qur'an" for emphasis, as you say: "Zayd came to me a righteous man, and 'Amr came to me a rational human being," so "a man" and "a human being" are for emphasis.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿without crookedness﴾. Ibn Abi Talhah related from Ibn Abbas that he said: "not created." Others said: "upright, not varying."

Ibn Abi 'Abla read: "salima li-rajulin" with a kasra on the sin and a damma on the mim. The rest read: "wa rajulan salaman" with a fatha on the sin and lam, [and with nasb] on both, and tanwin. Al-Zajjaj said: whoever reads "silman" and "salaman" — both are verbal nouns (masdar) described by them, so the meaning: "a man possessing peace toward a man and possessing a state of peace toward a man"; so the meaning is: possessing peace. **Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 39, verses 32–35**

(p-182) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So who is more unjust than one who lies about Allah﴾ by ascribing to Him a son and a partner, ﴿and denies the truth when it has come to him?﴾ That is the tawhid (the oneness of God) and the Qur'an. ﴿Is there not in Hell a residence for the disbelievers?﴾ That is, a station for those who deny? This is a rhetorical question that carries the sense of affirmation, meaning: indeed, it is so.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the one who brought the truth﴾ has four opinions.

The first: he is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. This was said by ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatada, and Ibn Zayd. Then, concerning the truth that he brought, there are two views. One is that it is "There is no god but Allah," narrated by Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Saʿid [ibn] Jubayr said likewise. The second is that it is the Qur'an, said by Qatada.

[Concerning the one who affirmed it there are three views. The first: he is also the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; he is the one who brought the truth, and he is the one who affirmed it. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Shaʿbi. The second: he is Abu Bakr, said by ʿAli ibn Abi Talib. The third: they are the believers, said by Qatada, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Zayd.]

The second opinion: the one who brought the truth is the people of the Qur'an, and the truth is that with which they will answer on the Day of Resurrection, and they have fulfilled its right. They are the ones who affirmed it. This was said by Mujahid.

The third: the one who brought the truth is the prophets. This was said by al-Rabiʿ. According to this view, the one who affirmed it is the believers.

The fourth: the one who brought the truth is Jibril (Gabriel), and the one who affirmed it is Muhammad. This was said by al-Suddi.

(p-183) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those are the God-fearing﴾, that is, those who guarded themselves against shirk (associating partners with Allah). It was said "they" because the meaning of "the one who" (alladhi) is plural in meaning. So the linguists said, and Abu ʿUbayda and al-Zajjaj recited:

Indeed those whose blood was spilled at Fulj, they are the people, all the people, O mother of Khalid.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That Allah may remove from them﴾. The meaning is: He gives them what they wish, so that He may remove from them ﴿the worst of what they did﴾, that is, to cover that by forgiveness. ﴿And reward them with their best deeds﴾ for their good works, not for their bad ones.

**Ibn al-Jawzi's commentary (Zad al-Masir) on surah 39, verse 42:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death﴾, meaning: He seizes the spirits at the time of the death of their bodies. ﴿And those that have not died﴾, meaning: and He takes those that have not died ﴿during their sleep﴾.

﴿Then He withholds﴾, meaning: from the body and the soul [and the self] ﴿those upon whom He has decreed death﴾. Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "qudiya" (قُضِيَ) with a damma on the qaf and a fatha on the ya', and "al-mawt" (المَوْتُ) in the nominative (بِالرَّفْعِ).

﴿And He releases the other﴾ back to the body ﴿until a specified term﴾, which is the end of the lifespan. ﴿Indeed, in that are signs for a people who reflect﴾ regarding the matter of resurrection.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: The spirits of the living and the spirits of the dead meet in the sleep, so they recognize one another and ask one another questions. Then the spirits of the living are returned to their bodies, and nothing of them is lost. This is His saying: ﴿Indeed, in that are signs for a people who reflect﴾.

Ibn Abbas also said in another narration: In the son of Adam there is a nafs (نَفْسٌ, self/soul) and a ruh (رُوحٌ, spirit). With the nafs is the intellect and discernment, and with the ruh is breath and movement. When the servant sleeps, Allah seizes his nafs and does not seize his ruh.

Ibn Jurayj said: In the human being there is a ruh and a nafs, and between them is a barrier. He, the Exalted, seizes the nafs during sleep and returns it to the body upon waking. But if He intends to cause the servant to die in his sleep, He does not return the nafs and seizes the ruh.

The scholars have differed as to whether there is a distinction between the nafs and the ruh, on two views, which I have mentioned in my book "al-Wujuh wa-al-Nazair" (الوُجُوهِ والنَّظائِرِ, *Aspects and Parallels*), and I have expanded on this verse in the chapter on *tawaffi* (بابِ التَّوَفِّي) in my book "al-Naza'ir" (كِتابِ "النَّظائِرِ").

Some scholars held that the *tawaffi* mentioned concerning the sleeper is his sleep itself. This is the view preferred by al-Farra' and Ibn al-Anbari. Accordingly, the meaning of the sleeper being "taken" (tuwuffiya, تُوُفِّيَ) is the seizing of his nafs from acting and exercising its faculties, and its "release" (irsaluha, إرْسالُها) is its being set free upon waking to act and exercise its faculties.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or have they taken intercessors?﴾ That is, the disbelievers of Makkah.

﴿Say: "Even though they possess nothing and do not understand?"﴾ That is, possessing nothing of intercession, and not understanding that you worship them?! The answer to this interrogative is omitted, its implied meaning being: "Even though they have this attribute, would you take them?!"

**Ibn al-Jawzi, Zad al-Masir, on Surah 39 (az-Zumar), verses 45–48:**

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And when Allah alone is mentioned, the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter shrink in aversion﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions.

The first is that they recoiled from *al-tawhid* (the affirmation of God's oneness). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. The second is that they became arrogant; this was said by Qatada. The third is that they took flight; this was said by Abu 'Ubayda and al-Zajjaj.

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿But when those besides Him are mentioned﴾, meaning the idols, ﴿behold, they rejoice﴾, meaning they are glad. The explanation of what follows has already been given [al-An'am: 14, 73; al-Baqarah: 113; al-Ra'd: 18], up to His words: ﴿And there will appear to them from Allah that which they had not reckoned﴾.

(p-188) As-Suddi said: They thought their deeds were good deeds, but there appeared to them evil deeds. Others said: They did deeds that they thought would benefit them, but they did not benefit them because of their polytheism. Muqatil said: There appeared to them, when they were raised, what they had not reckoned, namely that it was descending upon them.

This statement admits of two interpretations. The first is that they used to hope for nearness to Allah through worshipping the idols, but when they were punished for it, there appeared to them what they had not reckoned. The second is that resurrection and recompense had not been part of their reckoning.

It is related from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir that he panicked at the time of death and said: "I fear this verse, that there will appear to me what I do not reckon."

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And there befell them﴾, meaning there descended upon them ﴿that at which they used to mock﴾, meaning that which they used to deny and call a lie.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 39, verses 49–52:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So when harm touches man, he calls upon Us﴾. Muqatil said: He is Abu Hudhayfah ibn al-Mughirah, and a similar verse has already preceded in this surah [az-Zumar: 8]. He referred to the blessing with the words ﴿We have bestowed it﴾ only because the intended sense of "blessing" is bounty (in'am).

﴿On knowledge﴾ with me, meaning: on account of a good that God knew to be with me. It was also said: on knowledge from God that I am deserving of it. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Rather, it is a trial﴾, meaning the blessing with which God has favored him is a trial (fitnah), i.e., a test by which the servant is tried, to see whether he will be grateful or ungrateful. ﴿But most of them do not know﴾ that this is a gradual leading-on (istidraj) for them and a test. It was also said: "Rather, it is" refers to the statement that he uttered, [namely] "a trial."

﴿Already said it﴾, meaning that very word, which is his saying: "I have only been given it on knowledge," ﴿those who came before them﴾. There are two views concerning them. One: they are the past nations, as related by as-Suddi. The second: Qarun, as related by Muqatil.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So what they used to earn did not avail them﴾, meaning: it did not avert the punishment from them. ﴿What they used to earn﴾ — and concerning this there are three views. One: from disbelief. The second: from the worship of idols. The third: from wealth.

﴿So the evils of what they earned befell them﴾, meaning: the recompense of their evil deeds, which is the punishment.

Then He threatened the disbelievers of Makkah, saying: ﴿And those who wronged among these — the evils of what they earned will befall them, and they will not escape﴾, meaning: they cannot overpower God nor outstrip Him.

Muqatil said: Then He admonished them so that they would know His oneness, when they were given rain after seven years of drought, saying: ﴿Do they not know that God extends provision for whom He wills and restricts [it]? Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe﴾, meaning: in the extension of provision and its restriction.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 39, verse 60–61:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection you will see those who lied about Allah﴾, [claiming] that He has a son and a partner, ﴿their faces will be blackened﴾. Al-Hasan said: They are those who say, "If we wish, we act, and if we wish, we do not act." The rest of the verse we have already mentioned earlier [az-Zumar: 32].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah will deliver those who were righteous with their achievement﴾. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr, on the authority of Asim, read: "bi-mafazatihim" (with their achievements, in the plural). Al-Farra' said: It is like when you say, "The matter of the people and their affairs has become clear, and the voice and the voices have risen," and the meaning is one. Regarding it, the exegetes have three opinions. The first: with their virtues; this was said by as-Suddi. The second: with their deeds; this was said by Ibn as-Sa'ib and Muqatil. The third: with their salvation from the Fire.

Al-Mubarrad said: Al-mafazah is a noun of place (mafa'alah) from al-fawz (success). If it is made plural, it is good, as in your saying: "as-sa'adah" and "as-sa'adat" (happiness and happinesses). The meaning is: Allah will deliver them through their success, that is, through their deliverance from the Fire and their success in attaining Paradise.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 39, verse 62–63:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿To Him belong the keys (maqalid) of the heavens and the earth﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: That is, their keys (mafatih) and their treasuries (khaza'in), because the owner of the keys is the owner of the treasuries. Its singular is iqlid (key), and it is pluralized in the manner of non-singular forms, as they say: madhakir, the plural of dhakar. It is said that it is Persian, arabicized (mu'arrab). [And I read to our shaykh Abu Mansur al-Lughawi: al-iqlid is al-miftah (the key), a Persian word that has been arabicized.] The rajaz poet said:

؎ لَمْ يُؤْذِها الدِّيكُ بِصَوْتِ تَغْرِيدِ ولَمْ تُعالِجْ غَلَقًا بِإقْلِيدِ

Al-miqlid is a dialectal variant (lughah) of al-iqlid, and its plural is maqalid.

The exegetes differ regarding al-maqalid, in two sayings. One: the keys (al-mafatih), said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: the treasuries (al-khaza'in), said by al-Dahhak. Al-Zajjaj said: its explanation is that everything in the heavens and the earth, He is its Creator and the one who opens its door. The exegetes said: the keys of the heavens are the rain, and the keys of the earth are the plants.

Ibn Kathir recited "ta'murūnnī" with the nūn doubled (tashdid) and the yā' with a fatḥah. The rest recited with the yā' sukūn.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And it has certainly been revealed to you and to those before you﴾ There is an inversion (taqdīm wa ta'khīr) in it. Abu 'Ubaydah said: its figurative sense (majāz) is the figure of the two matters, where one is reported about and the other is withheld.

Ibn 'Abbas said: This is a form of discipline from Allah, may He be exalted, toward His Prophet ﷺ and a warning to others, because Allah, mighty and majestic, had already protected him from shirk. Others said: He addressed him with this only so that those other than him would know that shirk nullifies all previous deeds, even if it occurred from a prophet.

Abu 'Imran, Ibn as-Sumaif and Ya'qub recited "la-nuḥbiṭanna" with the nūn, and "'amalaka" with the accusative (naṣb).

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 39, verses 71–75:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who disbelieved will be driven to Hell in groups﴾. Abu 'Ubayda said: *al-zumar* (groups) are companies, with some following closely upon others. Its singular is *zumrah*.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Messengers from among you﴾, meaning from among yourselves. And ﴿the word of punishment﴾ is His saying: ﴿I will surely fill Hell﴾ [al-A'raf: 18].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Its gates will be opened﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read *futihat* and *futtihat* with the doubled *ta'* (shaddah). 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read them with the single *ta'* (without shaddah).

On this *waw* there are three opinions.

The first: it is redundant (*za'idah*). This is narrated from a group of the linguists, including al-Farra'.

The second: it is the *waw* of circumstance (*waw al-hal*). The meaning is: they came to it while its gates had already been opened. The *waw* was included to show that the gates were open before their arrival, and it was omitted in the account of the people of the Fire to show that they were closed before their arrival. The wisdom in this is of three aspects.

The first: the people of Paradise come to it when its gates have been opened, so that they hasten to joy and delight when they see the gates open. The people of the Fire come to it while its gates are closed, so that its heat is more intense for them. This was mentioned by Abu Ishaq Ibn Shaqla from our companions.

The second: standing at a closed gate is a kind of humiliation, so the people of Paradise are protected from it, while it is ascribed to the people of the Fire. This was mentioned to me by some of our shaykhs.

The third: if the people of Paradise found its gate closed, waiting for it to be opened would diminish the perfection of generosity. Part of the perfection of generosity is keeping the gate of the Fire closed until its people arrive, because the generous one hastens the reward and delays the punishment. Mighty and Majestic is He has said: ﴿Why would Allah punish you if you are grateful and believe?﴾ [al-Nisa': 147]. The author said: this is a weighty aspect in my view.

The third opinion: the *waw* was added because the gates of Paradise are eight and the gates of the Fire are seven, and the Arabs join numbers above seven with *waw*, as we mentioned in His saying: ﴿They will say, "They were seven, and their eighth was their dog"﴾ [al-Kahf: 22]. al-Tha'labi related this opinion and the one before it.

The scholars differed about where the response (*jawab*) of this verse lies, on three opinions.

The first: the response is omitted. This was said by Abu 'Ubayda, al-Mubarrad, al-Zajjaj and others. Concerning the estimate of this omitted element there are two views. One: its estimate is: ﴿until, when they come to it . . .﴾ to the end of the verse . . . they will be made happy. This was said by al-Mubarrad. The other: ﴿until, when they come to it﴾ up to His saying: ﴿Enter it, abiding forever﴾ . . . they entered it. It was omitted only because the speech contains an indication of it. This is the choice of al-Zajjaj.

The second opinion: the response is: "Its keepers will say to them," and the *waw* is redundant. This was mentioned by al-Akhfash, who said: a similar usage in poetry is:

*"So when that, O Kubayshah, was not but like the stammering of a dreamer in a fantasy."*

That is, "so when that . . ."

The third: the response is: "until, when they come to it, its gates are opened," and the *waw* is redundant. al-Zajjaj related this from a group of people of the language.

As for His saying: ﴿You are good﴾, there are five opinions.

The first: when they reach the gate of Paradise, they find beside its gate a tree from beneath whose trunk two springs flow. They drink from one of them, and whatever harm or impurity is in their bellies leaves. They wash in the other, and their skins never become dusty nor their hair disheveled ever again. Then, when they reach the gate of Paradise, its keepers say to them at that moment: ﴿Peace be upon you, you are good﴾. This was narrated by 'Asim ibn Damrah from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him. We have mentioned something similar from Ibn 'Abbas in [al-A'raf: 44].

The second: "Your dwelling is good," said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: "You are good through obedience to Allah," said by Mujahid.

The fourth: they were purified before entering Paradise by forgiveness, and retaliation was taken from some of them for others. When they were refined, the keepers said to them: "You are good." This was said by Qatadah.

The fifth: "You were good in the world," said by al-Zajjaj.

When they entered it, they said: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us﴾ of Paradise, ﴿and made us inherit the land﴾, meaning the land of Paradise, ﴿so that we may settle in it wherever we will﴾, meaning we may take for ourselves whatever dwellings we wish. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi related that the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ) will enter Paradise before the other nations, and they will settle wherever they wish in it, and then the other nations will settle in it after them. Therefore they said: "We settle in Paradise wherever we will." Mighty and Majestic is He says: ﴿How excellent is the reward of those who work﴾, meaning how excellent is the reward of the obedient in this world, which is Paradise.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And you will see the angels surrounding the Throne﴾, meaning encircling it. It is said: "The people encircled so-and-so" when they surrounded him. The *min* (from) was included for emphasis, as in your saying: "No one came to me."

﴿Glorifying their Lord with praise﴾. al-Suddi and Muqatil said: by the command of their Lord. Some of them said: they glorify Him with praise, when the monotheists enter Paradise. Ibn Jarir said: *tasbih* (glorification) here means prayer.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And it will be judged between them﴾, meaning between the creatures, ﴿with truth﴾, meaning with justice. ﴿And it will be said: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾ This is the saying of the people of Paradise, thanking Allah, may He be exalted, for His blessing.

The commentators said: Allah began the mention of creation with praise, saying: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who created the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-An'am: 1], and He concluded the matter, which is the settling of the two groups in their abodes, with praise to Allah in this verse. Thus He draws attention to praising Him at the beginning of every matter and at its end.
